fatal_errors: The proposed thermo-mechanical processing, annealing above 900 °C, or aging route is not the target condition; the reported alloy was produced by vacuum arc melting and evaluated in the as-cast context.

The falsification experiment uses tensile testing, whereas the target mechanical results are from room-temperature compression testing, preventing direct comparison with the reported yield strength and fracture strain.
A two-batch baseline-versus-Cr comparison does not cleanly separate changes in dendritic/interdendritic micro-segregation from effects of the Cr-induced Laves phase.

The sole cited evidence concerns different Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-X or Hf-Nb-Ti-V-Zr systems and annealing-induced C15 formation, so it does not directly validate the claimed phase, morphology, or mechanical mechanism in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-Cr.
explanation: The hypothesis reconstructs the central scientific picture well: approximately 4 at.% Cr, approximately 4 vol.% interconnected Laves phase, crack deflection/bridging, and Cr-induced BCC lattice contraction and solid-solution hardening. It also correctly makes reticulation and measurable contraction necessary boundaries. However, it replaces the target as-cast vacuum-arc-melted condition with an unsupported annealing or aging scenario and substitutes tensile testing for room-temperature compression. The outcome is only qualitative and omits the reported approximately 13.5% yield-strength increase, 20.6% fracture-strain increase, 1750.6 MPa yield strength, and 14.0% fracture strain. The boundary gives only a generic greater-than-0.1% contraction rather than the observed shift from about 3.392 to 3.325 Å. Finally, comparing only Cr-free and Cr-bearing specimens cannot independently identify whether behavior changed because of altered micro-segregation, dissolved Cr, or Laves-phase formation; matched controls or spatially resolved composition–phase–crack correlations would be needed.
